newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korea seen posting record trade deficit in 1996.
newsitem.headline: S.Korea seen posting record trade deficit in 1996.

text.p: South Korea is likely to post a record $19 billion trade deficit this year, almost double last year's shortfall, the trade ministry said on Wednesday.
Separately, the finance ministry said the year-on-year consumer price index rose 4.7 percent in the first nine months of this year, exceeding the government's 1996 target of 4.5 percent.
But a finance ministry official said there was no reason for concern.
"As we are expecting a good harvest this year, the targeted inflation rise for this year will be easily met," he said.
Trade ministry official Lee Jae-gil blamed the trade deficit on plunging international prices for semiconductors, steel and petrochemical products.
The ministry earlier predicted the annual deficit would reach $11-$12 billion.

"The revised forecast looks reasonable as the sluggish exports of semiconductors are expected to continue until the end of this year," said Rhee Namuh, head of research of Dongbang Peregrine Securities.

The September trade gap soared to $1.54 billion against $643 million a year earlier, but was sharply down on August's record $3 billion shortfall. Exports reached $9.84 billion and imports $11.38 billion.
September figures were helped by a generally lower trade volume because of the Korean Thanksgiving holiday, the trade ministry said.
The deficit totalled $14.96 billion for the first nine months of this year against $9.39 billion a year earlier.
"This is largely due to the plunge in semiconductor exports," Lee said.
Chip exports plunged 47.6 percent year-on-year to $1.13 billion in September.
The international spot price for 16-megabit dynamic random access memory (DRAM) chips stood at $11 in September, down 78.1 percent from a year ago. The August price was $12.

"I'm pessimistic over the economy this year," said Cho Dal-ho, economist at Samsung Economic Research Institute. "The recession, starting from the second half of last year, is likely to be prolonged."
He predicted South Korea's economy growth would be below 7.0 percent this year and inflation would exceed 5.0 percent. The government has targeted inflation at 4.5 percent.
The Korea Institute of Finance earlier forecast gross domestic product (GDP) would grow a real 6.6 percent this year, lower than the government's revised economic forecast of seven percent.
Anaysts said there were no short-term remedies.
"In fact, the government can do nothing as the current problem is caused by external shocks," Lee of Samsung said.
Korean products also have been hit by a weakening Japanese yen. Korea and Japan compete against each other in world markets with similar products.
Analysts said the impact of the won's depreciation against the dollar would show up from early next year, but the falling yen had already offset much of the potential competitive gains.
